title: Lesson 20: Governance and Guardrails: Acceptable Use, PII, and Responsible Automation
description: Writing a plain-language acceptable-use policy, treating personal data as a bounded resource held at the minimum the work needs, and building mechanical guardrails that enforce the policy even when nobody is watching.

questions.question: What distinguishes a guardrail from a policy rule?
options: A guardrail is written in more precise legal language than a rule
A guardrail is reviewed by the client while a rule is written by the agent
A guardrail is optional while a rule is mandatory
A guardrail is enforced by the platform regardless of the agent
questions.explanation: A guardrail does not rely on the agent choosing to behave; it mechanically refuses, which is what makes it hold under unattended operation.

questions.question: How should an agent handle personal data?
options: Give the agent all available context so its answers are more accurate
Hold the minimum the work needs and retrieve the rest on demand
Copy full records into its persistent memory for faster reuse
Store records in an external memory service without asking the client
questions.explanation: The safest personal data is the data you do not hold: keep only what the work needs, retrieve the rest on demand, and keep raw records out of persistent memory.

questions.question: What is the default for a dangerous command in an unattended run?
options: Auto-approve it so the unattended job never stalls
Prompt the client each time the command appears
Deny it so the unattended agent is blocked
Route it to the agent to judge whether it is safe
questions.explanation: The deny default keeps a recurring agent from silently picking up destructive commands when nobody is watching; it is a governance decision to keep.
